title: The diffusion coefficient from the jumps
spoken: D equals one over two tau times the integral, from minus infinity to infinity, of Delta squared times phi of Delta, d Delta.
explanation: D is the mean squared jump in one short interval, divided by twice that interval. Nothing about the fluid appears here yet; that comes with Stokes' law.
assumptions: Jumps in successive intervals are independent and symmetric, one coordinate.
These are modern teaching equations in SI notation, not a transcription of the printed paper.

notes.title: Over every jump
notes.explanation: Adds up the contribution of every possible jump, from any leftward to any rightward one.

notes.title: Per two intervals
notes.explanation: One over two tau turns a squared distance per jump into a rate.

notes.title: Times
notes.explanation: The rate factor times the averaged squared jump.

notes.title: What it asserts
notes.explanation: D is set by the jumps themselves: their mean square, per unit of time.

notes.title: Jump squared
notes.explanation: Squared, so leftward and rightward jumps both add.

notes.title: Two tau
notes.explanation: Twice the interval; the two comes from the second derivative of the density.

notes.title: Weighted by how likely
notes.explanation: Each squared jump counts in proportion to how often it happens.

notes.title: How likely a jump is
notes.explanation: Paper 2's phi: probability per metre of a jump of this size. A density, not a probability.

notes.title: Diffusion coefficient
notes.explanation: How fast the spread grows, in square metres per second. Not a speed.

notes.title: The short interval
notes.explanation: Paper 2's tau: short enough for the density to change little, long enough for jumps to be independent.

notes.title: A jump
notes.explanation: How far a particle moves in one interval tau.

notes.title: The jump it describes
notes.explanation: phi is read at this jump.

notes.title: Summed over jumps
notes.explanation: The variable the integral runs over.

sentence.text: times the mean of the squared jump
, each jump weighted by its density
